catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbate-giusep: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Giuseppe Baini, born in Rome in 1775 and dead there in 1844, traces the musician's career in the Roman School. Baini trained with his uncle Lorenzo Baini and later with Jannaconi, choirmaster of the Vatican Basilica. Jannaconi brought him into the Sistine Chapel choir as a bass singer. In 1818 Baini was elected its director, a post he held until his death. His works include a ten-voiced Miserere still sung in Holy Week. His lifework, though, was his 1828 memoir of Palestrina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-our-:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Our Lady of Gethsemani describes a Trappist abbey in Nelson County, Kentucky, the first abbey on American soil. On 26 October 1848 a colony of forty Trappists left Melleray in France under Dom Eutrope Proust, reaching New Orleans in early December and travelling by river to Louisville.

Bishop Flaget, who had long wished for their arrival, welcomed them, and on 21 December they took possession of their lands, soon joined by a second colony of twenty from the motherhouse. With indomitable energy the monks cleared the ground and raised an immense quadrilateral, one side formed by the church and the rest by monastic quarters and a guesthouse. A pontifical brief of July 1850 erected the new monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-trin: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on La Trinità di Cava describes a monastery near Cava dei Tirreni, in a gorge of the Finestre hills. Alferio Pappacarbona, a Salerno noble turned Cluniac monk, founded it in 980. Urban the Second endowed it richly, making it subject directly to the Holy See. Boniface the Ninth made it a diocese in 1394, though Leo the Tenth later detached Cava itself, and Cassinese monks replaced the Cluniacs. The abbey holds documents reaching to the 700s, and it now serves as a national school under Benedictine care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agostino-stef:
Agostino Steffani, Spiga's titular bishop, diplomatist, and musician, was born at Castelfranco in Treviso province in 1655. He died at Frankfort in 1728 or 1730. Twelve years old, Count Tattenbach brought him to Munich after hearing him sing at St. Mark's in Venice. At Bavaria's court he stayed twenty-one years, rising from chamber musician to director and court organist.

In 1688 he left Munich for Hanover's court, where he knew Leibniz intimately. In 1698 he settled at Dusseldorf. His compositions fall in three classes. First, religious music, including a Laudate pueri for nine voices and a Psalmodia Vespertina for eight. His Stabat Mater for six with orchestra drew praise that Scarlatti had produced nothing finer. Second, chamber duets, over a hundred preserved and esteemed the most perfect of their kind. Third, operas: five for Munich, nine for Hanover, and at least two for Dusseldorf. Diplomatic missions in 1696 and 1698 suited his gentle, prudent manners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albani:
The Albani were a distinguished Italian family said to descend from Albanian refugees who reached Italy in the fifteenth century. The family soon split into branches at Bergamo and Urbino, and gave the Church one pope, Clement XI, who reigned from 1700 to 1721, along with several well-known cardinals. The entry sketches its leading members one by one, from soldiers and statesmen to churchmen and patrons of learning.

Gian Girolamo of Bergamo, born in 1504, served Venice as a soldier, statesman, and canonist, an expert in church law. Annibale, a cousin of Clement XI, became Cardinal Bishop of Sabina and supported church literature, while his brother Alessandro also rose to the cardinalate. Giovanni Francesco became a cardinal at twenty-seven and later Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia. Giuseppe, made cardinal in 1801, sheltered in Vienna from 1796 to 1814 before returning to Rome after Napoleon's fall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-ma:
Alessandro Manzoni was an Italian poet and novelist, born at Milan in March 1785 and dead there in May 1873. He was the son of Pietro Manzoni, of a feudal family near Lecco, and Giulia, daughter of Cesare Beccaria. After schooling under the Somaschi and the Barnabites and a short stay at Pavia University, he grew up at Milan. His youth mixed study with dissipation. In 1805 he went to live with his mother at Paris, where he took in Voltairean ideas.

In 1808 Manzoni married Henriette-Louise Blondel, a banker's Protestant daughter. When she became Catholic at Paris in 1810, he followed her back into the Church. His creative work of 1812 to 1827 made him the voice of Italian romanticism, defended in his letter On Romanticism. His masterpiece, The Betrothed, dates from 1821 to 1825, with a rewrite in 1840. It tells of two peasants against Spanish oppression in Milan and the war of the Mantuan succession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-pi:
Alessandro Piccolomini was an Italian man of letters, philosopher, and astronomer, born in June 1508 and dead in March 1578. He spent his youth on literature, writing comedies, sonnets, and Italian verse translations of Ovid's Metamorphoses, part of the Aeneid, and Aristotle's Poetics and Rhetoric. He took the Padua chair of philosophy in 1540, writing there on the life of a nobly born man in a free city and on natural philosophy.

In his treatise on the size of the earth and the water, published at Venice in 1558, he fought the Aristotelian and Ptolemaic view. He argued that water does not cover more of the earth than land. The book sparked a controversy with Antonio Berga. In astronomy he held to the Ptolemaic theory, and he also wrote on reforming the calendar in 1578 and on Aristotle's mechanics. Gregory XIII made him titular Bishop of Patras in 1574 and coadjutor at Siena.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-ta:
Alessandro Tassoni was an Italian poet, born at Modena in 1565 and dead there in 1635. He spent his life serving prelates and princes in Italy as secretary or in similar posts. His fame rests chiefly on his mock-heroic poem The Stolen Bucket of 1614. It treats in mock-serious style a mighty struggle between two neighbouring towns over the theft of a well-bucket.

The comic and the serious blend skilfully through the poem, and the methods of ancient epic description are faithfully copied. The work stands with the ancient Battle of the Frogs and Mice, Lope de Vega's Gatomaquia, Boileau's Lutrin, and Pope's Rape of the Lock. Tassoni's dislike of the invading Spaniards shows in his Philippics against the Spaniards. His views on criticism appear in his Considerations on Petrarch's rhymes and his Diverse Thoughts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloisio-garde:
Aloisio Gardellini, born at Rome in 1759 and dead there in 1829, is famous for gathering the decrees of the Congregation of Rites. Before 1587 Mass and the sacraments had obeyed regulations from various popes. In time these grew confused through overlapping, amplification, and abolition. In that year Sixtus V, in the constitution Immensae aeterni Dei, created a body of cardinals, bishops, and clerics to guard proper celebration of the church offices.

A 1730 volume of papal regulations and congregational decrees by the Venetian priest John Baptist Pithonius fell short. Not until 1807 did Gardellini publish the first two volumes of his celebrated collection. A monitum to students of the rites was prefixed. Gardellini was a profound student of the liturgy, unexcelled in diligence, piety, and learning. His collection, comprising all decrees from 1602, grew by three volumes in 1816 and a sixth in 1819, with a few errors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anagni:
Anagni, an Italian diocese in the province of Rome under the direct rule of the Holy See, covers ten towns and claims an apostolic origin. Its bishops enter history in the fifth century. Felix attended the Lateran Synod of 487, and Fortunatus signed the acts of 499. Later bishops won special favour from the popes, among them Zachary, legate at Constantinople in 851 over the election of Photius.

Four popes came from Anagni and were related to one another: Innocent III, Gregory IX, Alexander IV, and Boniface VIII. Thomas Becket found shelter here in flight, and a chapel in the cathedral basement honours him. Boniface VIII was seized here by agents of Philip the Fair. At Anagni too, Alexander III excommunicated the Emperor Frederick Barbarossa and renewed the sentence on the antipope Victor IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-spagni:
Andrea Spagni, an educator and author, was born at Florence on 8 August 1716 and died at Rome on 16 September 1788. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1731 and taught philosophy and theology. For a time he taught mathematics at the Roman College and assisted Father Asclepi in astronomical observations.

His most noted work, De Miraculis, published at Rome in 1777 and revised in 1779 and 1785, sets out the doctrine of the nature and reality of miracles. With thoroughness it also gathers the rationalists' objections, from his own and earlier times, against the chief miracles of the Old and New Testaments. It stands as a compendium of the literature up to the last quarter of the eighteenth century. His other works form a Latin series from 1764 to 1781. They cover efficient cause, good, evil, and beauty, the world, the ideas of the human mind, motion, the souls of brutes, and the signs of ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-vanni:
Andrea Vanni, painter and statesman, was born at Siena in 1320 and died in 1414. He entered politics after the democratic overthrow of his city's government. A letter to him from Saint Catherine, his countrywoman and friend, on administration, still survives. He sat on the Grand Council and served as ambassador to the pope at Avignon and to Naples.

As an artist he weakly imitated Simone Martini and Lorenzetti. With Lippo Vanni, Bartolo di Fredi, and Taddeo di Bartolo, he carried Sienese art into the fifteenth century. His work, a polyptych in Santo Stefano at Siena, shows the Virgin enthroned between Stephen, James the Less, John the Baptist, and Bartholomew. Its small heads and gestures show a stiffness. A Madonna and Child in San Michele, a Birth of the Virgin joint with Bartolo di Fredi, and frescoes of Saint Catherine at San Domenico complete his known works. He painted at Naples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-maria-:
Angelo Maria Quirini, called Querini, cardinal and scholar, was born at Venice in 1680 and died at Brescia in 1755. In 1696 he entered the Benedictine order at Florence, becoming professor of Sacred Scripture there in 1705. Five years later he travelled through Germany, the Netherlands, England, and France.

In 1718 the pope put him on the Greek liturgical books commission, and in 1723 named him Bishop of Corfu. A few years later he moved to Brescia as cardinal. He headed the Vatican Library from 1730, later becoming prefect of the Congregation of the Index. He joined the Vienna Academy in 1747, the Berlin Academy in 1748. Opposing fewer holy days brought a controversy with Muratori, ended by Rome in 1750. His Aquileia part brought enforced retirement from Rome in 1751. He gave generously from his own means to German missions. His writings cover Greek liturgy and history, the papacy under Paul II, and an edition of Cardinal Pole's correspondence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-balle:
Born near Bologna in 1805 and dead in Rome in 1881, Antonio Ballerini spent his life as a Jesuit teacher of moral theology. That field is the study of right and wrong conduct in Catholic teaching. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1826 and taught philosophy, church history, and moral theology at Ferentino, Fermo, and the Roman College. He took part in sharp disputes over the writings of Rosmini, the moral system of Alphonsus Liguori, and the ties between bishops and religious orders, above all in England.

His writing also touched the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine that Mary was conceived free from original sin. He helped compile a menology, a calendar of saints' lives, for his order. A short handbook based on Gury reached seminaries in the United States in adapted form. His main work, a commentary on Busenbaum's Medulla, was finished and published by Palmieri after Ballerini's own work on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-marti:
Archbishop of Florence Antonio Martini, born at Prato in 1720 and dead in 1809, is remembered as the scholar behind a modern Italian Bible. After ordination he directed the Superga College at Turin. There Cardinal delle Lanze urged him to meet Pope Benedict XIV's wish for a good version of Scripture in current Tuscan speech. The New Testament, translated from the original Greek, proved too much beside his college duties, so he resigned the directorship for a state council post and pension.

He finished publishing the New Testament in 1771, then worked on the Hebrew Old Testament with help from Rabbi Terni, a Jewish scholar. Pope Pius VI approved the whole work, praised Martini in person, and made him archbishop of Florence in 1781. In that office he partly blocked a garbled edition of his Bible, and a third authorized edition came from his own archiepiscopal press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolicae-s:
Apostolicae Sedis Moderationi is a bull of Pius IX, issued 12 October 1869, that recast the system of censures and reserved cases in the Catholic church. It serves in practice as its present penal code. Though the church's founder is divine, its members are human, with human passions, so it needs laws to guide them and penalties to correct them. Over centuries penal statutes piled up, some confirming, some changing, some repealing earlier laws.

The Council of Trent, meeting from 1545 to 1563, simplified them, but new laws then accumulated again until canonists grew confused, moralists perplexed, and the faithful hesitant. Pius IX therefore simplified three hundred years of accumulation in a single bull. The entry explains why a church needs a penal code, how its code grew tangled, and what the 1869 reform set in order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assemani:
Assemani, Arabic Sam'an, or Simeon, is the name of a renowned Maronite family of Mount Lebanon in Syria. Four of its members, all clergy, distinguished themselves in the eighteenth century in East and West. For zeal, learning, and unbounded attachment to Rome, popes held them in great esteem and gave them many well-merited dignities and offices.

Oriental studies, above all Syriac studies, owe them more than any others. Through their research, manuscript collecting, and voluminous publications, Syriac studies and the history, saints' lives, liturgy, and literature of eastern churches were first introduced into Europe. They can justly count, if not as creators, certainly as the most renowned pioneers of modern Oriental studies, preceded by other Maronite scholars known under Latin names such as Echellensis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustino-old:
Augustino Oldoini was an Italian historian and bibliographer, born in 1612, who died at Perugia in 1683. He came from La Spezzia and entered the Society of Jesus in 1628. After the usual studies in humanities, philosophy, and theology, he taught classics at Perugia and then moral philosophy in its theological school. His first work, on hard points of Latin grammar, appeared at Ancona in 1637 while he was teaching humanities.

His later years went to history and bibliography, above all to the popes and cardinals. He prepared a new annotated edition of Ciacconius's History of the Popes, in four volumes issued at Rome between 1670 and 1677, reaching to Clement IX. Around it he published a necrology of popes and antipopes, a work on Clements famed for holiness, and his Roman Athenaeum, a survey of writings by popes, antipopes, and cardinals. He also issued Athenaeums for Perugia and for Liguria in 1680.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balthasar-bon:
Balthasar Boncompagni was an Italian mathematician born at Rome in 1821, who died in 1894. His family had given the Church Gregory XIII, reformer of the calendar. He learned mathematics and physics under Santucci and grew into a prolific writer on both subjects and their history. At nineteen he published biographical sketches in the Giornale Arcadico and a paper on definite integrals in Crelle's Journal.

In 1846 the same journal printed his study of physics advances in Italy across the sixteenth and eighteenth centuries. He joined the Accademia dei Lincei in 1847 and soon became its librarian. In 1868 he founded the Bolletino, a journal for the history of mathematics, which he ran until 1887. Its essays covered translators like Gherardo of Cremona and Leonardo, and in 1857 he published a Cambridge manuscript held to translate Al-khwarizmi's arithmetic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barnaba-orian:
Barnaba Oriani was an Italian Barnabite priest who studied the stars, born near Milan in 1752, who died at Milan in 1832. Educated by Barnabites at Milan's San Alessandro College, he joined the order and was ordained at twenty-three. Shortly after, in 1776, he joined the staff of Milan's Brera Observatory, becoming assistant in 1778 and director in 1802. From 1778 he published papers on the stars in the Effemeridi di Milano for fifty-two years.

A 1785 memoir working out Uranus's path won him a high place among star scholars, and he declined Palermo's astronomy chair. He toured Europe's chief star centers at state expense, and under Napoleon refused to swear hatred of monarchy. The government softened his oath, kept him at Brera, and made him head of the weights and measures board. With De Cesaris he measured the arc between Rimini and Rome, and he worked thirty-seven years with Piazzi, who found Ceres.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barnabas-of-t:
Barnabas of Terni was a Friar Minor and missionary, of the noble Manassei family, who died in 1474 or 1477. A Doctor of Medicine learned in letters and philosophy, he spurned worldly honors to join the Umbrian Friars Minor. He preached with wonderful success until severe illness stopped him, and served in many offices with prudence and kindness. He zealously promoted the Observance branch of the order.

His lasting honor is founding the first monte di pietà, a charitable loan institution shielding the poor from crushing usury. After consulting the jurist Fortunatus Coppoli and winning wealthy Perugians' support, he opened the first at Perugia in 1462. Violent opposition failed against him at a public disputation, and other cities soon took up the work. Great Franciscan missionaries spread the monti, which wonderfully improved Italy's social conditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-battista-guar:
Battista Guarini was an Italian poet born at Ferrara in 1538, who died at Venice in 1612. His father Francesco was a great-grandson of the humanist Guarino da Verona, founder of the family's Ferrara fortunes. After academic years at Padua and Ferrara, he entered Alfonso II's court in 1567 and served as diplomatist, notably in failed bids for Poland's crown in 1574 and 1575.

His domestic life was stormy: his daughter Anna was murdered by her husband with a son's help, and lawsuits embittered his career. His fame rests almost wholly on the Pastor Fido, a lyrical pastoral drama rivaling Tasso's Aminta. Published late in 1589 and often staged, it crowns Italian Renaissance pastoral poetry with shepherds' loves in an imaginary Arcadia. He also wrote lyrics, the comedy Idropica, a dialogue on secretaries, and a treatise backing Medicean Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bellini:
Giacomo Bellini, father of the painters Gentile and Giovanni, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born about 1400 and dead by 1471, he matters most as the teacher who shaped the founders of the Venetian school of painting. His own surviving pictures are few and, by the entry's judgment, minor.

His sketchbook draws the warmer praise, holding copies of ancient statues, Bible scenes, Christian legends, and lively drawings from nature. The entry also sets him against the rival Vivarini painters and notes his work in Venice and beyond. It is a short life of an artist known mainly through his sons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-jus:
Benedetto Justiniani, also spelled Giustiniani, was a Jesuit writer on theology and the Bible, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Genoa about 1550, he died at Rome in 1622 after a career spent teaching and preaching. He entered the Jesuits at Rome in 1579 and taught rhetoric and theology in Rome, Toulouse, and Messina.

For more than twenty years he headed the Roman College and served as chief preacher to the pope. Pope Clement VIII also sent him as theologian to Cardinal Cajetan during a mission in Poland. His two great works explain the letters of Paul and the Catholic epistles, and the entry presents them as solid, learned commentaries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-men:
Benedetto Menzini, a priest and poet of Florence, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1646 to a poor family, he died at Rome in 1704 after a life spent teaching, writing, and seeking patronage. Early work as a teacher of fine letters led to chairs at Florence and Prato, and later to Rome under Queen Christina of Sweden.

His poems fill the second half of the entry, from heroic odes on Venice and Budapest to elegies, pastoral sonnets, and light lyrics. A poem on the earthly paradise continues Tasso's world, while his satires attack the hollow verse of his day. The entry presents a sharp, learned poet who never quite won the post he wanted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-sest:
Benedict Sestini, a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1816, he died in Maryland in 1890 after a career split between Rome and America. He joined the Jesuits in 1836, studied at the Roman College, and worked as assistant at the Roman Observatory under Father De Vico.

The revolution of 1848 drove him from Rome to Georgetown College, and later to Woodstock, Maryland. His star-colour catalogue, the first broad survey of the heavens by star colour, is his chief scientific work. In later years he also led the Messenger of the Sacred Heart and its prayer league, joining mathematics with devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-lu:
Bernardino Luini, a Milanese painter, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born between 1470 and 1480, perhaps at Luino, he died after 1530. Even his name is unsure: he signed himself Lovinus, and Vasari calls him del Lupino in one place and di Lupino in another. By 1507 he was a master with many commissions.

No proof makes him Leonardo's pupil, though his Virgin and Child pictures and his Christ Crowned with Thorns come very close to Leonardo in colour and feeling. Luini's own mark is sweetness and intense devotion, without Leonardo's mysterious smile or pagan tinge. The entry presents a gentle painter living in a giant's shadow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-ippolito-g:
Blessed Ippolito Galantini, founder of Florence's Congregation of Christian Doctrine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Florence in 1565 to obscure parents, he died in 1619. A childhood cure turned his mind to God's service, and he taught Christian doctrine in the Jesuit church while still a boy.

At twelve he won Archbishop Alexander de' Medici's notice, who gave him the church of Santa Lucia al Prato for his work. Between silk-weaving, his trade, and teaching poor children and adults, he built a congregation of lay catechists. The entry presents a working man turned apostle of Christian teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-colom:
Blessed John Colombini, founder of the Jesuati, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Siena about 1300 to an old patrician family, he died on the road to Acquapendente in 1367. Early life showed no seed of holiness: commerce swelled his fortune, and fellow citizens repeatedly elected him gonfalonier, or chief magistrate.

Avarice marred a fortunate marriage until sickness and grace turned him. He left his luxurious house for a poor hospital ward, then made his home a refuge for the needy, washing their feet with his own hands. Eight years of conversion later he founded the Jesuati, a congregation of lay penitents. The entry presents a merchant turned servant of the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-bapti:
Blessed Baptista Varani, an ascetical writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born Camilla Varani at Camerino in 1458, daughter of Duke Julius Caesar Varano and Joanna Malatesta, she died there in 1527. Little is known of her first ten and last twenty-three years; her middle years survive almost entirely through her own writings.

Her confessor, Blessed Peter of Mogliano, drew from her a spiritual autobiography of visions, penance, and devotion to Christ's passion. Entering the Poor Clares, she founded a convent at Camerino and wrote for her sisters. The entry presents a duchess's daughter who wrote her own soul's history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-clare:
Blessed Clare of Rimini, of the Poor Clares, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Rimini in 1282, she died there in 1346. Early loss of parents and a pious husband left her exposed to the dangers of youth and beauty. She fell into sinful dissipation. Then a voice at Mass in the Friars Minor church bade her say one Our Father and Hail Mary with fervour.

Reflection followed, and she took the Third Order habit, then founded a convent of Poor Clares, working miracles and growing in contemplation toward life's close. Her body rests in Rimini cathedral, and Pius VI approved her cult in 1782, with a feast on 10 February in city and diocese. The entry presents a sinner turned foundress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bonifazio-vit:
Bonifazio Vitalini, a Mantuan jurist turned priest, wrote on criminal law and canon law across a long career. Born at Mantua about 1320, he studied law at Padua and practiced criminal law, publishing his Super maleficis. He then left the law for the priesthood and left Padua, though he came back in 1350 as rector and bishop's vicar.

Two years later he went to Avignon, taught there, and rose through curial offices: prothonotary apostolic, advocate of the consistory, fiscal of the curia, and auditor of the sacred palace. He was still at Avignon in 1388. His works include a commentary on the Clementines and treatises on procedure against apostates and on cases needing a special mandate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brunetto-lati:
Brunetto Latini, Florentine philosopher and statesman, taught Dante and brought oratory and political science into Florentine public life. Born at Florence about 1210, son of Buonaccorso Latini, he worked as a notary and shared in the 1250 revolution that broke Ghibelline power. Sent in 1260 to Alfonso X of Castile for aid against Manfred, he learned on his return that the Guelphs had lost at Montaperti and fled.

At Paris a generous countryman kept him while he studied and worked as notary, and he dedicated his Tresor to that friend. After the Guelph triumph of 1266 he returned to Florence, served as secretary to the Commune, and shaped republican counsels. His French prose Tresor encircles all mortal knowledge, while his earlier Italian Tesoretto, an allegorical poem of Nature, Virtues, Love, and Olympus, plainly influenced Dante, who meets him in Inferno canto fifteen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cajetan-bedin:
Cajetan Bedini, Italian cardinal and diplomat, was born at Sinigaglia on 15 May 1806 and died at Viterbo on 6 September 1864. Pius IX made him Commissary Extraordinary at Bologna in 1849, while revolt shook the Papal Provinces. In 1853, as nuncio to Brazil, he was sent to visit the United States and call on President Franklin Pierce.

His courtesy visit was misread as a bid for diplomatic recognition, and his tour drew anti-Catholic protests throughout, stirred by Italian exiles, the apostate priest Gavazzi, and the Know-Nothings. A plot to kill him failed, and at Cincinnati a plot against him and the cathedral ended in rioting and bloodshed. He left America in January 1854.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camillus-tarq:
Camillus Tarquini, cardinal, Jesuit canonist and archaeologist, was born at Marta on 27 September 1810 and died at Rome on 15 February 1874. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1837, having already published a doctoral thesis on canon law. He held the Roman College chair of canon law, winning notice for his masterly expositions of Scripture at the Gesù.

His treatise on the royal placet for papal bulls, published in 1851 and translated into German, Spanish, and French, forms an appendix to his chief work on public church law of 1862. That work ran through fourteen editions. As an archaeologist he wrote on Etruscan inscriptions, monuments, and language, including an Etruscan grammar and dictionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-goldoni:
Carlo Goldoni was a Venetian dramatist born in February 1707 who died at Paris in January 1793. He remade the Italian theatre by replacing improvised commedia dell'arte with fully worked character plays after Molière, filled with realism drawn from close watch of Italian life. His French Mémoires of 1787 tell his life in detail and recount his fight to improve the repertory against Chiari and Gozzi.

As a boy he followed his physician father through Perugia and Rimini and ran off with a theatrical troupe. He then studied law and served as assistant to a criminal-court clerk at Chioggia. A law degree and advocacy in Venice followed, with playwriting throughout. Later editions of his works ran to 44 volumes in 1795 and 46 volumes in 1817 to 1822, a measure of his standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caroline-book:
The Caroline Books, or Libri Carolini, form a work in four books and some 120 chapters. It claims Charlemagne as author and dates from about 790 to 792. It is a severe critique of the Seventh General Council at Nicaea in 787, above all on sacred images, and a weighty theological treatise in its own right. Both the Iconoclast council of 754 and its opponent, the Second Nicene council, stand judged equally wrong before Frankish criticism.

The first erred, in this judgment, by barring all images as sheer idolatry, while the second erred by urging absolute adoration of images. Learning far beyond Charlemagne's known powers points to another author, perhaps Alcuin or a Spanish or Irish theologian at court. The work grew from a faulty Latin version of the Greek acts. A dropped negative and copyists' slips made the council seem to demand worship of images as of the Trinity itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cavaliere-gio:
Born in Rome in 1571 and dying there in 1644, Baglioni was a painter of distinction, nicknamed the Deaf Man of the Barozzo. His paintings, however, are overshadowed by his biographies of his contemporaries. His chief literary work is his Lives of painters, sculptors, and architects of Rome, covering 1573 to 1642, spanning the reigns from Gregory XIII through Urban VIII.

A pupil of Francesco Morelli, Baglioni painted in Rome for Sixtus V, Clement VIII, and Paul V in turn, working notably in the Vatican, St. Peter's, and St. John Lateran. Paul V honored him with knighthood in the Order of Christ, given for his painting of St. Peter raising Tabitha, now lost. His Last Supper survives at San Nicolo in Carcere, with a St. Stephen at Perugia and a St. Catherine at Loreto.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestino-cav:
Celestino Cavedoni was an Italian ecclesiastic, archaeologist, and numismatist, born at Levizzano-Rangone near Modena on 18 May 1795 and dying at Modena on 26 November 1865. After seminary studies he distinguished himself at Bologna from 1816 to 1821 in archaeology and in Greek and Hebrew. He then became custodian of Modena's numismatic museum and joined the city library, rising to librarian in 1847.

Between 1830 and 1863 he held the hermeneutics chair at the University of Modena. He served as a corresponding member of the commission Napoleon III created to edit the works of Count Borghesi, adding many scientific notes. His numismatic works include studies of Roman family medals, old Italian coin tables, and biblical numismatics, and in 1863 he published a refutation of Renan's Life of Jesus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-bianc:
Charles Bianconi was a merchant and philanthropist born in the duchy of Milan in 1785 and dead near Clonmel, Ireland, in 1875. Sent young to Ireland to apprentice with an Italian printseller, he became a wealthy merchant. Between 1815 and 1858 he built the first system of rapid and cheap transport across the whole island. It carried people and government mail. O'Connell counted him an intimate friend, and he promoted Catholic Emancipation, backed many Catholic charities, and supported the Catholic University at Dublin in practical ways.

The English postmaster general reported in 1857 that no living man had done more for the benefit of the sister kingdom. Bianconi showed extraordinary energy and ingenuity in building his vast transport system, increasing his adopted country's resources and knitting its social relations. His Longfield home near Clonmel welcomed guests and served the general welfare in practical ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-of-ri:
The Council of Rimini opened in early July 359 with over four hundred bishops, the Western half of Constantius's twin attempt to settle the Arian strife. An Eastern synod met in parallel. At Rimini, some eighty Semi-Arians withdrew from the orthodox majority, leaving Restitutus of Carthage among its leaders, while exiled Nicene bishops stayed away.

Both parties sent deputations to the emperor. The orthodox professed the faith of Nicaea, while the minority backed the imperial formula drafted by Marcus of Arethusa, which dropped the word essence as unscriptural and divisive. Hasty adoption and lack of papal approval left the result without authority, and Jerome's verdict stands: the whole world groaned to find itself Arian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-gino-ca:
This biographical entry follows Count Gino Capponi, a Florentine historian and man of letters born in 1792 and dead in 1876, whose life joined scholarship, travel, and moderate politics. Trained by private tutors in the humanities and in English, French, and German, he travelled widely in Italy and abroad, befriending the exiled poet Foscolo in England.

Back in Florence he helped launch influential periodicals, including the Antologia in 1821 and the Archivio Storico Italiano in 1842, and kept company with the best scholars of his day. In the troubled year 1848 his prudence carried him to head the Grand Duchy's ministry, and he later sat as a senator. Blindness darkened his final years, spent in study and memoir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cyril-sieni:
A biographical entry follows Cyril Sieni, better known as Cyril of Barcelona, a Capuchin missionary bishop in Louisiana. Born in Catalonia at an unknown date, he died after 1799. In 1772 the Bishop of Santiago sent him to New Orleans as vicar-general. Louisiana then lay within Santiago's rule.

Church conditions were poor, and the local Capuchin superior had set governor and people against him. As titular Bishop of Tricali and auxiliary of Santiago, Cyril governed seventeen parishes and twenty-one priests across Louisiana, Alabama, Florida, and the Mississippi valley. He sent pastors to Saint Louis, Pensacola, and Saint Augustine. In 1786 he issued a letter on keeping Sunday holy. Despite errors in rule, he was esteemed a holy, simple-minded man.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-combon:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Comboni, missionary to Central Africa, born near Brescia in 1831 and dead at Khartoum in 1881. Schooled at Mazza's Institute in Verona, he learned languages and medicine, was ordained in 1854, and first reached Central Africa in 1857 before ill health sent him home in 1859. His 1864 Plan for the Regeneration of Africa launched years of fundraising across Europe.

In 1867 he founded at Verona his Institute for African missions, with a sister institute for women, and opened houses at Cairo to season missionaries for fever country. As pro-vicar apostolic from 1872 and vicar apostolic from 1877, he ruled a vicariate of nearly 100 million souls from just two missions, growing it steadily. He checked the slave trade through the khedive and Sudan's governor, and his institute still carries on his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-bern: Domenico, son of famed artist Giovanni Lorenzo Bernini, lived during the eighteenth century's early years. He became a prelate and canon of Saint Mary Major in Rome and gave himself to church history. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry lists his chief works. They include a four-volume history of the heresies printed at Rome from 1705 to 1717, memoirs of popes in wars against the Turks, and a study of the Roman Rota tribunal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egidio-forcel:
Egidio Forcellini was an Italian maker of Latin dictionaries, born at Fener near Treviso in 1688 and dead at Padua in 1768. His parents were poor, so he came late to schooling and entered the Padua seminary in 1704. There his teacher Facciolati saw his ability and industry and set him to help revise Calepinus, the Latin dictionary in seven languages.

While at that task Forcellini dreamed of a new Latin lexicon, the fullest ever made. From late 1718 he read through the whole of Latin literature and all the inscriptions, pausing from 1724 to 1731 to teach rhetoric and run the seminary at Ceneda. His great Totius Latinitatis Lexicon, giving Italian and Greek equivalents with full citations, came out at Padua in four folio volumes three years after his death. It remains the base of Latin dictionaries still in use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ang:
Francesco Angiolini, born at Piacenza in 1750 and dead at Polotsk on 21 February 1788, was a noted Jesuit scholar of unusual range. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1765 and, after its suppression, retired to Polotsk. He wrote poems of his own in Italian, Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, comedies in Polish, and a Polish grammar for Italians, showing a gift for languages that crossed the usual scholarly borders.

His translations are his chief monument. He put Sophocles' Electra, Oedipus, and Antigone into Italian, Thucydides into Italian, left incomplete, Sophocles into Polish, and Josephus into Italian in three volumes published at Florence between 1840 and 1844. The entry lists him among the learned Jesuits whose work survived the order's suppression, carried on in exile and in print long after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-ber:
Francesco Berni, born at Lamporecchio near Florence in 1497 or 1498 and dead at Florence on 26 May 1535, was an Italian comic poet of the Renaissance. The son of noble but poor parents, he struggled in Florence until Rome offered better luck. Cardinal Bibbiena, Angelo Dovizi, and Giovanni Matteo Giberti, Bishop of Verona and datary to Leo X, employed him in turn. The datary kept him at correspondence all day and frowned on his clowning.

Freedom came at Padua in 1531, where he traded insults gaily with the notorious Aretino. A pleasing post followed in 1533, when Cardinal Ippolito de' Medici made him a canon of Florence cathedral. That easy life lasted only two years: caught in the feud between Ippolito and Alessandro de' Medici, he died of poison under mysterious circumstances. His great work refashioned Boiardo's Orlando innamorato, published at Milan seven years after his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-bia:
Francesco Bianchini, born at Verona on 13 December 1662 and dead at Rome on 2 March 1729, was a student of the natural sciences and a historian of wide honour. He began with mathematics, physics, and astronomy, later studied theology, became a deacon in 1699, and never took priesthood. Moving to Rome in 1684, he found a protector in Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni, whose library he kept, and Ottoboni's favour continued when the cardinal became Pope Alexander VIII.

Bianchini served later popes as president of the society for historical antiquities in 1703, secretary of the commission for reforming the calendar, and envoy carrying a cardinal's hat to France. Learned men there received him with respect and Oxford paid his stay in England. Benedict XIII made him historiographer of the Lateran synod of 1725. His epitaph praised a great purity of life and exceeding modesty of mind, and he belonged to many learned academies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-bor:
Francesco Borromini, born at Bissone on 25 September 1599 and dead by his own hand at Rome on 1 August 1667. He was an architect and sculptor who became the boldest voice of the Roman baroque. He studied under Carlo Maderna, a relative, and on Maderna's death became architect of St. Peter's under Bernini, his great rival. His most extravagant work was San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane, built between 1640 and 1667, a full expression of the developed baroque style.

At the College of Propaganda his fancies ran wildest, while the cupola and campanile of Sant' Andrea delle Fratte show better taste. His modernised nave of St. John Lateran and facade of Sant' Agnese in Piazza Navona count among his best work. The entry judges him harshly, calling him the father of modern abuses in architecture, for overturning Greek and Roman rules without offering a substitute, yet his buildings remain unmistakable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-giu:
Francesco Giuseppe Bressani, born at Rome on 6 May 1612 and dead at Florence on 9 September 1672, was a Jesuit missionary to the Indians of New France. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1626, studied at Rome and Clermont, and taught at Sezza, Tivoli, and Paris before sailing for America. After serving the French at Quebec, he was sent to the Algonquins at Three Rivers. In April 1644, on his way to the Huron mission, the Iroquois captured and cruelly tortured him for over two months.

Ransomed by the Dutch at Fort Orange, he reached France in November 1644, yet returned to Canada the next year. He laboured on the Huron mission until the Iroquois destroyed it four years later, then ministered to scattered Huron fugitives. Failing health sent him back to Italy in 1650. His Breve Relatione of 1653 remains a first-hand account of the missions, translated into French at Montreal in 1852.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-gui:
Francesco Guicciardini, born at Florence in 1483 and dead there on 23 May 1540, was a historian and statesman of the Italian Renaissance. Born to ancient Florentine families attached to the Medici, he began as a successful lawyer and married Maria Salviati in 1508. In 1511, though legally too young, he was sent as Florentine ambassador to the King of Spain. On his return he entered Medici service, then the service of the Church, governing Modena and Reggio well under Leo X and defending Parma against the French in 1521.

He helped Clement VII form the League of Cognac in 1526 and served as lieutenant-general of the army that could not prevent the sack of Rome in 1527. After shifting between republican and Medici loyalties, he returned to Florence in 1530 and joined its government. His Storia d'Italia and his Ricordi, counsels and reflections, remain classics of political history, admired for cool judgment and hard-won experience.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-van:
Francesco Vanni, born at Siena in 1565 and dead there in 1609. He was a painter of the Eclectic School who many regard as a restorer of sixteenth-century Italian painting. His first teachers were Salimbene and Passarotti. He studied Raphael at Rome under de' Vecchi, but that style did not please Siena. He went to Parma and Bologna and took up the manner of Baroccio, the Umbrian leader of the baroque style. Through teaching and example he left a lasting influence, training capable pupils including his sons Michelangelo and Raffaello.

Called to Rome by Clement VIII on the recommendation of Baronius, he painted his best work, the great altarpiece for St. Peter's showing Simon Magus rebuked by St. Peter. Its colours survive remarkably well. The pope rewarded him well and made him a knight.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-furni: Furni was a titular see in Roman Africa where two towns shared the name. One, found at El-Msaadin near Tebourba, had a bishop, Geminius Victor, as early as the third century, and another, Simeon, sat at Carthage in 525. The second Furni, at Henchir-Boudja near Zama, sent a Donatist bishop to the synod of Carthage in 411. Its gate is linked to the martyr Mansuetus of Urusi, burned alive there, and its churches burned in the persecution of 305.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaetano-moron:
Gaetano Moroni, author of the great Dictionary of Historical-Ecclesiastical Learning, rose from a barber's shop to the papal household. Born at Rome in 1802 and schooled by the Christian Brothers, he was apprenticed to a barber whose rounds took him to the Camaldolese house of San Gregorio. There Abbot Mauro Cappellari spotted his gifts and put him to secretarial work.

When Cappellari became Gregory XVI, Moroni served as his chamber aide and private secretary, writing over 100,000 letters, and he later served Pius IX the same way. From convent books, talk with learned men, and his own notes he built the Dictionary, issued at Venice from 1840 to 1861. Working alone, sometimes sixteen hours a day, he made it a mine of fact on court, Curia, and Papal States.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gasparo-conta:
Gasparo Contarini, a Venetian statesman and cardinal born in 1483, sought reform of the Church from within. Schooled at Padua in Greek, mathematics, and philosophy, he entered Venice's Great Council and served as ambassador to Charles V from 1520, reaching Worms in April 1521 as Luther's name spread. He never met Luther, but reported fully to the Senate on his return.

Made cardinal by Paul III in 1535, Contarini pressed the pope to curb abuses and choose worthy cardinals. He chaired the 1536 commission whose Counsel on Reforming the Church, issued early in 1537, laid bare Curial ills. His counsel to the pope was plain: do not abuse the vast power in your hands. He died at Bologna in 1542, a reformer who stayed loyal to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gasparo-luigi:
Gasparo Spontini, a composer born near Jesi in 1774, ruled Parisian opera with La Vestale and Fernand Cortez. Meant for the Church, he chose music instead, trained at Naples, and wrote six operas by 1799. After succeeding Cimarosa at Palermo in 1800, he settled at Paris in 1803, where Milton in 1804, La Vestale in 1807, and Cortez in 1809 fixed his fame.

Spontini led Italian opera at the Odéon from 1810, then served as chief Kapellmeister at Berlin from 1820 on a handsome salary. His Olympie, failed at first, won praise after revision in 1826, and Agnes von Hohenstaufen followed in 1829. The pope made him Count of Saint Andrea in 1844. Proud and prickly, he still left all his wealth to charity at his death in 1851.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gethsemani:
Gethsemani is the olive grove at the foot of the Mount of Olives where, in the Gospels, Jesus suffered his Agony and was arrested. Its Hebrew name joins words for press and oil, pointing to the olive trees planted there. A Catholic Encyclopedia article gathers what each Gospel calls the place, from a field or estate to a garden across the brook Cedron.

Early Christians kept visiting the spot, and pilgrims from the fourth century onward left accounts of its church and grotto. The Church of the Agony rose there and fell to the Persians in 614. It rose again under the Crusaders before it was razed around 1219. Its foundations were later found near the present garden. Seven old olive trees still stand in a square enclosure nearby, with a rocky grotto where tradition places the apostles' wait and the prayer on the eve of the Passion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giambattista-:
Giambattista Belzoni was an Egyptian explorer born at Padua in 1778, who died in Africa in 1823. A barber's son meant for his father's trade, he left home at fifteen and drifted to Rome, where he studied hydraulics. After wanderings through Holland and the British Isles, where need drove him onto the pantomime stage, he reached Egypt. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his turn from showman to excavator.

At the pasha's request he first tried a scheme to raise Nile waters at Zubra, but the authorities dropped it. He then hauled the colossal bust of Memnon, now in the British Museum, from the sands and explored up the Nile. He opened the pyramid of Chephren, found the mummy of Psammethis, and crossed Fayum, Libya, and desert oases. He published his travels in London in 1821, and died of fever on a later African journey toward Timbuktu.

Giambattista Pianciani was a Jesuit scientist born at Spoleto in 1784, who died at Rome in 1862. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1805, taught mathematics and physics across the Papal States, and then lectured at the Roman College for twenty-four years. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents him as a working physicist who also wrote on philosophy and religion.

The Revolution of 1848 cut his scientific work short and drove him from Rome to America. There he taught dogmatic theology at Georgetown during 1849-50, then returned in 1851 to administration and philosophy teaching. His books include a four-volume physical chemistry, a commentary on the Mosaic history of creation written at Georgetown, and philosophical essays of 1855 and 1856. His articles treated electricity and magnetism above all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gioacchino-an:
Gioacchino Antonio Rossini was an Italian opera composer born at Pesaro in 1792, who died at Passy near Paris in 1868. He trained at Bologna, found his first successes at Venice and Milan, and became the chief operatic composer of his time. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents him as a great innovator who opened a new road in musical art.

In serious opera he replaced long recitatives with more singing. In comic opera he set a new comedy style, adding fresh instruments to Italian orchestras. Tancredi of 1813 made him famous across Europe, and the Barber of Seville and Cenerentola followed in 1816 and 1817. Semiramide of 1823 was his last Italian opera, and William Tell of 1829, written for Paris, was his last opera of all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giordano-ansa:
Giordano Ansaloni, sometimes called Giordano di San Stefano, was a Dominican missionary born at San Angelo in Sicily early in the seventeenth century, who died in Japan in November 1634. After studies at Salamanca he sailed for the Philippines in 1625. As chaplain in a Manila hospital for Chinese and Japanese, he mastered both languages. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him into the Japanese persecution.

In 1631 he volunteered for Japan and arrived as the persecution broke out in 1632. Disguised as a Buddhist priest, he traveled the country giving the sacraments in secret. Seized in August 1634, he endured seven days of torture and was forced to watch the beheading of his companion and sixty-nine other Christians. He was then hung head-down from a plank until dead. On his way east he had written lives of Dominican saints in Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Guglielmini was a scientist born at Bologna in 1763, who died there in 1817. Known as the first scientific experimenter on the mechanical proof of the earth's rotation, he took the tonsure young with the title of Abate but took no higher orders. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his careful falling-body trials in Bologna's Asinelli tower.

In 1789 he published reflections on a new experiment for the earth's daily motion. Between June and September 1791 he dropped sixteen balls from 241 feet, finding mean eastward and southward drifts close to his computed values. His skill became a model for Benzenberg and Reich, and his errors prodded Gauss and Laplace toward the true theory of motion on a moving earth. He taught mathematics at Bologna for twenty-three years.

Giovanni Battista Morgagni, called by Virchow the father of modern pathology, was an Italian physician born at Forlì in 1682, who died at Bologna in 1771. His father died young, and his mother gave her life to her gifted son's schooling. At Bologna he studied under Albertini and Valsalva, becoming the latter's special assistant in anatomy. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a life of direct observation.

He founded a student society, the Academy of the Restless, for men unsatisfied with book knowledge who wanted science from observation and experiment. At Padua he wrote his great book On the Seats and Causes of Disease, published at Venice in 1771, which laid the foundation of modern pathology. He held tuberculosis contagious, distrusted bloodletting, and studied the pulse and aneurisms with lasting value.

Giovanni Battista Moroni was a painter born at Bondo near Albino, in Bergamo territory, between 1520 and 1525, who died at Bergamo in 1578. Pupil of Alessandro Bonvicino, called Moretto da Brescia, he worked chiefly at Bergamo and nearby. A Catholic Encyclopedia article ranks him a portraitist not inferior to his master, with the same sincerity and nobility but more originality.

His portraits stand among the most vigorous of the Renaissance. A Scholar with an open book and a Man in Black hang at the Uffizi, and the Tailor hangs at the National Gallery in London. In religious pictures he falls below Moretto in drawing and invention, though his clear grayish coloring pleases. His Coronation of the Virgin for Bergamo's Trinity church and his Last Judgement at Gorlago show his sacred work at its best.

Giovanni Battista Rinuccini was a papal nuncio born at Rome in 1592, who died at Fermo in 1653. Son of a Florentine patrician, he took his doctorate at Pisa at twenty-two and became Archbishop of Fermo in 1625. After twenty quiet years as a hard-working pastor, he was sent in 1645 as nuncio to Ireland. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his mission among a divided people.

Irish Catholics, maddened by oppression, had taken up arms and set up their own assembly and government at Kilkenny. Rinuccini arrived late in 1645 with arms, ammunition, and money, urging them to back the king against the Puritans in return for repeal of the penal laws. But Anglo-Irish and Old Irish split over peace or war, Ormond gave no toleration, and Rinuccini left in 1649, retiring to Fermo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-cont:
Giovanni Contarini was an Italian painter of the Venetian school, born at Venice about 1549, who died in 1605. A contemporary of Palma Giovine, he studied Tintoretto and Titian closely and was called an exact imitator of Titian. A Catholic Encyclopedia article tells the old story of his portrait of Marco Dolce, which the sitter's dogs mistook for their master.

His work is mannered, soft, and sweet, yet rich and beautiful in color, painted much on Titian's lines. His finest picture, now in the Louvre, shows the Virgin and Child with St. Mark and St. Sebastian. The Doge Marino Grimani kneels before them. He spent years at the court of Emperor Rudolf II, who knighted him, and his Resurrection in San Francesco di Paolo at Venice can claim to be masterly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-dome:
Giovanni Domenico Cassini was an astronomer born at Perinaldo near Nice in 1625, who died at Paris in 1712. After Jesuit schooling at Genoa, he turned from astrology to serious astronomy. In 1650 he took the astronomy chair at Bologna, left vacant by Cavalieri's death. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an observer whose calm, religious temper bore even total blindness cheerfully.

Called to France in 1669, he lived from 1671 in the Paris observatory built partly under his direction, and became a naturalized Frenchman in 1673. He fixed the rotation periods of Jupiter, Venus, and partly Mars from spots on their disks, and added four satellites to Saturn's one known moon. He studied the moon's librations, the zodiacal light, and comets, and his lunar names endure.

Giovanni Domenico Costadoni, known in religion as Dom Anselmo, was a Camaldolese monk, historian, and theologian born at Venice in 1714, who died there in 1785. Son of a rich merchant, he gave up worldly prospects for the habit at St. Michael's on Murano. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar whose literary gift showed at twenty-three in defense of Camaldolese writers.

For eighteen years he worked with Mittarelli on the Annals of the Camaldolese. They were published at Venice between 1755 and 1773. He wrote archaeological papers, practical counsels for religious, consoling letters, and letters on theological questions. After his death his unpublished manuscripts passed to St. Gregory's monastery at Rome by order of the abbot who later became Gregory XVI.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-gius:
Giovanni Giustino Ciampini was an ecclesiastical archaeologist born at Rome in 1633, who died there in 1698. He graduated in law from the Roman University, but soon gave himself to antiquities, an office in the Apostolic Chancery leaving him free to pursue them. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a collector and circle-builder who kept alive the school of Panvinio and Bosio.

He gathered books, coins, and statues with ardor. He founded a society for church history in 1671 and an academy of sciences in 1679 under Queen Christina of Sweden. His two lasting illustrated works treat the churches built by Constantine the Great and the art of mosaic. Both preserve, in pictures and learning, ancient buildings and mosaics that have since perished or decayed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-lore:
Giovanni Lorenzo Bernini was one of the most vigorous and fertile of Italian architects and sculptors, born at Naples in 1598, who died at Rome in 1680. His father, a painter and sculptor, gave him his first lessons, and in 1608 took him to Rome. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a baroque master who ruled art like a second Michelangelo, though in a style little like his.

At fifteen he carved the David with a Sling now in the Villa Borghese. In 1629 he became architect of St. Peter's and superintendent of public works in Rome. Under Paul V and his successors he rose to fame. Louis XIV honored him richly on a visit to Paris in 1665, though jealousy blocked his Louvre plans. He finished St. Peter's as its seventh architect, and died as rich as he was famous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-mari:
Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni was an Italian historian of literature, chronicler, and poet born at Macerata in 1663, who died in 1728. Educated at Rome for law, he gave most of his time to poetry and letters, took his doctorate in 1679, and became canon of Santa Maria in Cosmedin in 1705. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a critic whose prose outshone his verse.

His greatest work, the six-volume History of Vulgar Poetry of 1698, traces the origin and growth of Italian poetry. It weighs its hundred chief poets in order, and discusses the art and kinds of verse. It was followed in 1702 by five volumes of commentaries. He also founded the Academy of Arcadia in 1690 and presided over it until his death, pressing a simpler, more natural style against the perverted taste of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-pole:
Giovanni Poleni was a marquess, physicist, and antiquarian born at Venice in 1683, who died at Padua in 1761. Son of Marquess Jacopo Poleni, he studied classics, philosophy, theology, mathematics, and physics. At twenty-five he became professor of astronomy at Padua, then of physics in 1715 and of mathematics in 1719. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar trusted by kings and senates alike.

The Venetian Senate charged him with the waters of lower Lombardy and with flood defenses, and sovereigns called him to settle disputes over waterways. In 1748 Benedict XIV summoned him to Rome to examine the crumbling cupola of Saint Peter's, and he promptly named the needed repairs. Padua made him magistrate, erected his statue by Canova after his death, and Venice honored him with a medal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-sant:
Giovanni Sante Gaspero Santini was an astronomer born at Caprese in Tuscany in 1787, who died at Padua in 1877. Taught first by his uncle, the Abate Giovanni Battista Santini, he left law at Pisa for mathematics and the natural sciences. In 1806 the Italian government made him assistant at the Padua observatory, which he directed from 1814. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a long-lived observer who made Padua famous.

He took charge of an observatory housed in an old fortified tower, with a Ramsden mural quadrant as its best instrument. He set to work on comets, planets, planetoids, occultations, and eclipses, and in 1811 fixed the latitude of Padua by Gauss's method. He held the university chair of astronomy from 1813, served twice as rector, and directed mathematical studies from 1845 to 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-vill:
Giovanni Villani was a Florentine historian born about 1276, who died of the plague in 1348. Descended from a wealthy merchant family, he spent his life in commerce with the Peruzzi company and later the Bonaccorsi. He served as prior several times, worked at the mint, and guarded the fortifications. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the most modern of medieval historians.

At Rome in 1300 he conceived his chronicle of Florence in twelve books, running from the Tower of Babel to his own day. Early parts follow his authorities without much judgment, but from the middle of the thirteenth century the work becomes an excellent source. He records prices, state finances, and statistical detail, and, though a Guelph and a Black, does not hide wrongs done by his own party.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-vinc:
Giovanni Vincenzo Bolgeni was a theologian and controversialist born at Bergamo in 1733, who died at Rome in 1811. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1747, taught theology and philosophy at Macerata, and stayed in the Society until its suppression by Clement XIV. Pius VI made him Theologian-Penitentiary for his fight against Jansenism and Josephinism. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a fighter of no mean controversial talent.

His best known and least fortunate work, Della carità o amor di Dio of 1788, argued that charity is loving God as good to us, not as absolute goodness. Former Jesuit comrades and others attacked him, and he answered first with subtlety, then with silence. His later defense of probabilism stirred a fresh storm, and a treatise on usury published under his name after his death was probably not his.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-and-:
Girolamo and Pietro Ballerini were celebrated theologians and canonists, sons of a distinguished surgeon of Verona. Girolamo was born at Verona in 1701 and died in 1781; Pietro was born in 1698 and died in 1769. A rare intellectual sympathy bound the brothers, who helped each other prepare their many works. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows two lives spent in learned editions and disputes.

Together they brought out a complete edition of Cardinal Noris in 1729 to 1733 and an edition of Bishop Giberti in 1733. A critical edition of the sermons of Saint Zeno followed in 1739. Pietro defended Probabiliorism against the absolute Probabilists in three volumes, and fought the Laxists on usury. His monumental three-volume edition of Saint Leo, Rome 1753 to 1757, refuted Quesnel and closed with a profound study of the sources of canon law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-benz:
Girolamo Benzoni was a Milanese traveler born about 1519, who went to America in 1541 and returned to Italy in 1556. His travels took in the Antilles and the Isthmus, Guatemala, and South America's west coast, where he traded with difficulty as a foreigner in Spanish colonies. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a witness whose hatred of Spain shaped his famous book.

His Historia del Mondo Nuovo, published at Venice in 1565, was dedicated to Pius IV. It attacked Spain in America in a string of diatribes and accusations. It drew wide attention in the hottest phase of the controversy over the treatment of the Indians, and was quickly reprinted and translated. The book holds interesting firsthand detail, but abounds in errors and intentional misstatements, and its reports on Mexico and Peru bristle with mistakes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuliano-cesa:
Giuliano Cesarini, also known as Cardinal Julian, was born at Rome in 1398 and died at Varna in Bulgaria in 1444. Educated at Perugia in Roman law, he taught there with Domenico Capranica and Nicholas of Cusa among his pupils. Martin V created him cardinal in 1426 and sent him to Germany to preach a crusade. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a brilliant cardinal of the Western Schism's close.

As president of the Council of Basle he resisted Eugene IV's attempt to dissolve it. He withdrew from the opposition in 1437 when it sought to humiliate the pope rather than reform. At Ferrara and Florence he led talks with the Hussites and the Greeks toward reunion. As legate to Hungary in 1443 he persuaded King Ladislaus to break the peace of Szegedin and renew war, a step that ended in the disaster at Varna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-albero:
Giulio Alberoni was a cardinal and statesman born on 30 May 1664 at Firenzuola in the duchy of Parma, who died on 26 June 1752 at Piacenza. Son of very poor parents, he labored as a farm hand until fifteen, then became bellringer at Piacenza cathedral. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a rise from poverty to prime minister of Spain.

The Duc de Vendôme took him to Paris in 1706, and after his patron's death Alberoni became agent of the Duke of Parma at Madrid. He arranged the 1714 marriage of Philip V to Elisabetta Farnese, became prime minister, duke and grandee of Spain, and Bishop of Malaga, and was made cardinal in 1717. His reforms built manufactures, a mail service to the colonies, and a navigation school. His foreign policy aimed at recovering Spain's lost Italian lands, and ended in his fall in 1719.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-bian:
Giuseppe Bianchini, also spelled Blanchini, was an Italian Oratorian and scholar of the Bible, history, and church worship born at Verona in 1704, who died at Rome in 1764. Clement XII and Benedict XIV, who prized his learning, entrusted him with several learned tasks. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar whose great Bible work stayed unfinished.

His planned Vindiciae Canonicarum Scriptuarum Vulgatae latinae editionis was to run to several volumes, but only the first appeared at Rome in 1740, holding fragments of the Hexapla. More important is his two-volume Evangeliarium quadruplex of 1749, on the ancient Latin versions. His chief work on church rites, the Liturgia antiqua hispanica of 1746, covers the old Spanish, Gothic, Isidorean, Mozarabic, and Toledan rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-camp:
Giuseppe Campani was an Italian optician and astronomer who lived at Rome during the latter half of the seventeenth century. With his brother Matteo Campani-Alimensis he ground and polished lenses, especially those of great focal length and slight curvature. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a craftsman whose lenses powered Cassini's discoveries.

These lenses served long telescopes of considerable power, and Cassini made his discoveries with them. Campani also observed himself, and disputed with Eustachio Divini the priority of the spots on Jupiter, to which Cassini had called his attention. His observations and telescope descriptions appear in papers of 1664, 1665, and 1666, including letters to Cassini on the shadows of the Medicean stars on Jupiter's face.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-cata:
Giuseppe Catalani, also called Catalano or Catalanus, was a Roman liturgist of the eighteenth century and member of the Oratory of San Girolamo della Carita. He is famous for correct editions of the chief liturgical books of the Roman Church, still in habitual use, enriched with scholarly commentaries on their history, rubrics, and canon law. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an editor of lasting authority.

Among his editions are the Pontificale Romanum in three volumes of 1738 to 1740, based on the best manuscripts. His Caeremoniale episcoporum dates to 1747, and his Rituale Romanum to 1757. He also wrote on the history, duties, and privileges of two curial offices. He edited the decrees of the ecumenical councils in a work Hurter calls very learned. His 1753 edition of Aguirre's collection of Spanish and New World councils served scholars of the Americas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-mari:
Giuseppe Maria Bernini was a Capuchin missionary and Orientalist born near Carignan in Piedmont, who died in Hindustan in 1753. For many years he served as a missionary in the East Indies and gained a remarkable knowledge of the languages and dialects of India. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a traveler who studied the peoples he met.

In his travels he studied closely the manners, customs, and religious beliefs and practices of the people. He gathered the results in his Notizie laconiche of 1747 on customs, sacrifices, and idols in the kingdom of Neipal. Never published, it is kept in manuscript at the Propaganda in Rome and in Cardinal Borgia's museum. He also wrote Dialogues in an Indian language, translated the Adhiatma Ramayana and the Djana Sagara, and compiled historical studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-pari:
Giuseppe Parini was an Italian poet born at Bosisio on 23 May 1729, who died at Milan on 15 August 1799. Taken early to Milan, he showed marked ability for teaching, the work of most of his life, and entered the Arcadia on his poetic talent. Ordained in 1754, he tutored noble families and learned the fashionable life he would satirize. A Catholic Encyclopedia article rests his fame on the Odi and the Giorno.

From 1773 he taught fine arts at the Brera in Milan. Bonaparte made him a member of the municipal government under the Cisalpine Republic, a post he lost for his liberal utterances. The Giorno, begun about 1760, follows a society beau through morning, midday, evening, and night in unrhymed ten-syllable verse, mocking the effeminate and corrupt customs of fashionable youth. His Odi of 1791 treat moral and social questions in the conventional Arcadian manner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-tart:
Giuseppe Tartini was a violinist, composer, and theorist born at Pirano in Italy on 12 April 1692, who died at Padua on 16 February 1770. He resisted his parents' wish that he enter the Franciscan Order, studied law at Padua from 1710, then gave it up for music and fencing. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows one of the greatest violin players of all time.

After fleeing to Assisi over a secret marriage and a charge of abduction, later dropped, he returned to Padua. He settled for years at Ancona. In 1721 he became solo violinist and orchestra conductor at Padua Cathedral, a post he held for life apart from two years at Prague. His Padua school of 1728 produced masters such as Nardini, and his manner of bowing is still standard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-zamb:
Giuseppe Zamboni was a priest and physicist born at Venice in June 1776, who died there on 25 July 1846. After studies at the Verona seminary he took the chair of physics in the city's lyceum. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the inventor of the dry pile that still rings bells at Oxford.

His dry pile of 1812 stacked paper discs, zinc foil on one face and manganese binoxide on the reverse, with the paper's own moisture serving as conductor. Pressed in a glass tube, the stack gave force enough to deflect an electroscope's leaves. With a light brass ball swinging between the terminal knobs he made an electric clock. At Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory such a pile has rung bells continuously for fifty years, though it is no perpetual motor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregario-meng:
Gregario Mengarini was a pioneer missionary of the Flathead tribe and philologist of their language, born at Rome on 21 July 1811, who died at Santa Clara, California, on 23 September 1886. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1828 at barely seventeen and taught grammar at Rome, Medina, and Reggio. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a volunteer moved by the Flatheads' appeal.

Hearing Bishop Rosati's letter read in the refectory in 1839, he volunteered at once. He was ordained in March 1840 and sailed from Leghorn in July with Father Cotling. With De Smet's party he journeyed by river and trail to Fort Hall in August 1841. Then he reached the Saint Mary's River site in Montana, where the missionaries cut frozen earth with axes to found a log mission plastered with clay and thatched with weeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorio-panz:
Gregorio Panzani was Bishop of Mileto, who died early in 1662. A secular priest of Arezzo who had left the Oratory for ill health, he was chosen by Cardinal Barberini in 1634 for a secret agency in London. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a man of experienced virtue, singular address, and polite learning.

His commission was to report firsthand on divided English Catholics. He was to settle differences between seculars and regulars over the oath of allegiance and a vicar Apostolic, and open informal relations with the government. He reconciled seculars with Benedictines and other religious, but the Jesuits stayed out. He met secretaries Windebank and Cottington, won the queen's confidence, and was admitted to secret audience with the king. Elected Bishop of Mileto on 13 August 1640, he left memoirs whose authenticity was later questioned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-of-ri:
Gregory of Rimini was an Augustinian theologian born at Rimini in the second half of the thirteenth century, who died at Vienna in 1358. After teaching at home he was called to Paris to a professorship at the Sorbonne, where he won great distinction as a teacher. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a chief leader of the Nominalists.

His disciples called him Doctor acutus, Lucerna splendens, and especially Doctor authenticus, and many called him beatus for his erudition and heroic virtue. A pertinacious champion of Saint Augustine on grace and original sin, he opposed the general Scholastic teaching, even against the Aegidian school he belonged to. His opponents called him Infantium Tortor, tormentor of children, for his severe view of unbaptized children. He became General of the Augustinian Hermits in 1357 and died the next year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guido-reni:
Bologna's Guido Reni, born at Calvenzano in 1575, was once among the most prized painters in Europe, though fashion later dimmed his name. Trained by Calvaert and the Carracci, he worked in Rome on the Farnese and Quirinal palaces and Borghese chapel. His ceiling of Phoebus and the Hours before Aurora in the Palazzo Rospigliosi stands as his Roman high point.

Early pictures show pure colour and dramatic force, while later success brought a fluent but thinner manner that has hurt their survival. An engraver and etcher as well as a fresco and panel painter, he left works scattered from Dresden and St. Petersburg to many English country houses, and the entry expects his skill in composition and drawing to win fresh regard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-coena-domi:
In Coena Domini names a papal Bull read each year in Rome on Maundy Thursday, the feast of the Lord's Supper. In St. Peter's loggia, before pope, cardinals, and Roman Court, an auditor of the Sacred Roman Rota read it in Latin, and a cardinal-deacon then read it in Italian. Once read, the pope threw a burning wax torch down into the piazza.

Inside were excommunication censures for many offences, with absolution kept to the pope alone. Publishing censures on a set cycle was an old habit. In 1195 York's council told priests to proclaim censures on perjurers three times a year, with bell and lit candle. London's council in 1200 ordered yearly proclamation against sorcerers, perjurers, arsonists, thieves, and rapists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bellarin:
John Bellarini was an Italian Barnabite theologian best known as a moral theologian of the Counter-Reformation. Born at Castelnuovo in 1552, he served as visitor and twice as assistant general of his order. At Padua and Rome he taught theology. Bishops and cardinals held him in high esteem, particularly Gregory XV.

His most valuable work is a two-part commentary on the Council of Trent, and on the Roman Catechism. One volume instructs the faithful in the Apostles' Creed; it was published at Brescia in 1603. Another, aimed at converting heretics, was published at Milan in 1620 and often reprinted. He also wrote Italian booklets for confessors and penitents, a treatise on St. Thomas's doctrine of predetermination, a work on method, and a Mirror of Divine and Human Wisdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-cassan:

Born at Madrid in 1673, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1686 and became an Academy member in 1713. He worked on the Academy's great Dictionary of the Castilian Language, published in six volumes from 1726 to 1730.

Cassani was a prolific author on saints' lives, fortification, and comets. His most valued book for Americans is his 1741 history of the Jesuit province of New Granada, the only regular chronicle of the order in Colombia. Though he never crossed the Atlantic, the work gives a careful account of missions in the upper Orinoco basin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-pitoni:

He directed choirs at Monte Rotondo and Assisi, returned to Rome in 1677, and became director of St. John Lateran in 1708.

In 1719 Pitoni became choirmaster of St. Peter's, a post he held for twenty-four years. He could write each voice part separately without a full score, and his output, much of it for three and four choirs, was called infinite by his pupil Chiti. He began a Mass for twelve choirs but age kept him from finishing it. He died at Rome in 1743.
